tagline: Israel's book of practical wisdom: a father's instruction and hundreds of short sayings on living well in God's world, all rooted in the fear of the LORD.
overview:
Proverbs is a collection of collections. It opens with nine chapters of longer poems in which a father urges his son to choose wisdom over folly, and in which Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman, calls out in the streets and invites the simple to her table. From chapter 10 on, the book becomes mostly single sayings, usually two lines long, on speech, work, money, friendship, anger, family, justice, and the king. It ends with the words of two otherwise unknown sages, Agur and King Lemuel, and a closing poem in praise of a woman of noble character.

The book's motto comes in its first chapter: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). Wisdom in Proverbs is not cleverness or book learning. It is skill in living, the ability to see how God's world actually works and to act in step with it. That skill starts with reverence for God, and it reaches into the most ordinary places: how you talk, how you handle a loan, whether you get out of bed, how you treat a neighbor or a poor man at the gate.

Proverbs matters because most of life is ordinary. The Bible has great stories of exodus and exile, but it also has this book, which assumes that the God who made the world cares how a young man spends his evenings and how a merchant weighs his grain. It trains the reader to notice consequences, to value character over quick gain, and to see daily choices as moral and spiritual choices.
author:
The book names several authors. The heading at 1:1 attributes the proverbs to Solomon son of David, and headings at 10:1 and 25:1 name him again, the second noting that the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied those sayings. Two sections are credited more generally to “the words of the wise” (22:17) and “sayings of the wise” (24:23). Chapter 30 is the words of Agur son of Jakeh, and 31:1-9 the words of King Lemuel, taught him by his mother; neither man appears anywhere else in Scripture, and their home is uncertain. 1 Kings 4 remembers Solomon as a man of great wisdom who composed three thousand proverbs.

Traditional readers have taken Solomon as the source of the book's core, with other material added by later collectors. Many modern scholars think the Solomonic headings honor Solomon as the patron of Israel's wisdom tradition rather than claiming he wrote every line, and they see the book as the product of scribes and teachers over several centuries. Both views agree the book is openly edited: it tells us that Hezekiah's scribes gathered part of it, and it includes material from sages outside Israel's royal court.
date: The book grew over time, and its own headings show that. Solomon reigned in the tenth century BC, and material associated with him could go back to that era. Hezekiah reigned in Judah around 715 to 686 BC, so the collection in chapters 25 to 29 was copied down at least that late. The final form, including the opening nine chapters and the closing sections, is dated differently by different scholars. Some place the completed book in the late monarchy, before the Babylonian exile; many place its final editing in the Persian period after the exile, in the fifth or fourth century BC. Individual sayings are nearly impossible to date, since proverbs circulate orally for generations before anyone writes them down.
setting:
Wisdom literature was an international genre in the ancient Near East. Egyptian scribes produced books of instruction in which a father or official teaches his son how to succeed and behave rightly, and Mesopotamian texts collected proverbs and advice as well. The closest parallel to anything in the Bible is the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, a work published in the 1920s, whose content closely resembles Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22 at several points. Proverbs 22:20 speaks of “thirty sayings”, and Amenemope is arranged in thirty chapters. Most scholars conclude that Israel's sages knew and adapted this Egyptian work, reshaping its advice under the fear of the LORD.

Inside Israel, proverbs would have been taught in the home, where the book pictures father and mother instructing their children, and likely also among royal scribes and counselors who served the king. The world the book assumes is a small agricultural and commercial society: fields and harvests, city gates where elders judged cases, markets with weights and measures, loans secured by pledges, and a king whose justice set the tone for the land.
purpose: The prologue (1:2-6) states the aim: to give wisdom, discipline, and insight; to teach righteousness, justice, and fairness; to make the simple prudent and the young discerning; and to add learning even to the wise. The first readers were young men being formed for adult life, household, trade, and public service, and the opening chapters address a son directly. But the book also expects the mature to keep learning, and its sayings apply to anyone who has to decide how to speak, spend, work, and treat others. Its deepest purpose is to show that ordinary life belongs to God and that walking in his ways is the path of life.
story: Proverbs doesn't advance the Bible's plot the way Genesis or Kings does, but it is anchored in that story. It is tied to Solomon, the son of David, whose reign in 1 Kings 3 and 4 opens with a prayer for wisdom and a reputation for it that reached the nations, and whose later life shows how a wise man can still turn to folly. It assumes the covenant God of Israel, called by his name the LORD, and it echoes the law's call to bind God's words on the heart (Deuteronomy 6). Alongside Job and Ecclesiastes, it forms the Old Testament's wisdom writings: Proverbs states how life ordinarily works under God, and Job and Ecclesiastes press on the cases where it doesn't seem to. In the Hebrew Bible it sits in the third division, the Writings; in Christian Bibles it follows Psalms.
christ:
The New Testament quotes Proverbs several times. Hebrews 12 applies Proverbs 3:11-12 on the LORD's discipline to Christians who suffer, and James 4 and 1 Peter 5 both use the thought of Proverbs 3:34 that God gives grace to the humble. Paul calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30) and says that in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). Jesus himself said that one greater than Solomon had come (Matthew 12:42).

The portrait of Wisdom in Proverbs 8, present with God before creation and rejoicing in his work, shaped how the New Testament speaks of Christ as the one through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:15-17), though the chapter itself is a poetic personification, not a prophecy. Christians see in Jesus the one who lived the life Proverbs describes perfectly, and who is himself the wisdom the book's father urges his son to seek.
reading:
Read Proverbs as proverbs. A proverb is a compressed observation about how life usually goes under God, not a promise or a guarantee for every case. “Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (10:4) is true as a pattern, and the book knows it has exceptions: it speaks of the poor who are oppressed and of wicked men who prosper for a time. The clearest signal is 26:4-5, where two proverbs placed side by side give opposite advice about answering a fool. Wisdom lies in knowing which one fits the moment. The same applies to sayings like 22:6 on training a child: they describe the normal fruit of faithful parenting, not a contract that makes parents solely responsible for a grown child's choices.

Watch for the two paths and the two women, Wisdom and Folly, that frame the book's opening; for the recurring figures of the simple, the fool, the mocker, the sluggard, and the righteous; and for parallelism, where the second line of a saying repeats, contrasts with, or extends the first. Read the sayings slowly and a few at a time. Many readers take one chapter a day, which fits a book of thirty-one chapters.

structure.title: A father's instruction and Wisdom's call
structure.summary: A prologue stating the book's purpose, then a series of longer poems in which a father urges his son toward wisdom and away from violent men and the adulterous woman, with speeches by Wisdom herself, including her place at creation in chapter 8.

structure.title: The proverbs of Solomon
structure.summary: The largest collection: several hundred mostly two-line sayings, many built on the contrast between the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the foolish, covering speech, work, wealth, family, and the king.

structure.title: The words of the wise
structure.summary: Two shorter collections of longer sayings, the first closely related to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, with advice on the poor, rulers, drunkenness, and laziness.

structure.title: Proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men
structure.summary: A second Solomonic collection gathered in the days of King Hezekiah, rich in comparisons from nature and daily life and in counsel about kings and fools.

structure.title: The words of Agur and Lemuel
structure.summary: Agur's humble confession and his numerical sayings, followed by a queen mother's counsel to her son the king on wine, women, and justice for the poor.

structure.title: The woman of noble character
structure.summary: An acrostic poem, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, praising a capable woman who fears the LORD, closing the book as it began, with wisdom embodied.

themes.title: The fear of the LORD
themes.body: The book's foundation, stated at 1:7 and again at 9:10, is reverent awe toward the LORD, the God of Israel. This fear isn't terror but a settled recognition of who God is, which shows itself in humility, obedience, and turning from evil. Wisdom in Proverbs is never simply shrewdness; it grows from this root, and the book returns to it at its close in the praise of a woman who fears the LORD.

themes.title: Two ways
themes.body: Proverbs pictures life as a road with two paths: the way of wisdom and righteousness, which leads to life, and the way of folly and wickedness, which leads to death. Choices that look small, a companion, a loan, a glance, a lie, set a person on one road or the other. The book trains the reader to see where a path ends before stepping onto it.

themes.title: Wisdom personified
themes.body: In chapters 1, 8, and 9, wisdom speaks as a woman who calls in public places, offers life and favor, and was present with God when he made the world. Her rival, Folly, also calls to passers-by. The personification makes the choice concrete and personal: to choose wisdom is to accept an invitation to a relationship, not only to master a set of rules.

themes.title: Words and speech
themes.body: Few subjects get more attention in Proverbs than the tongue. The book contrasts honest and lying lips, gentle and harsh answers, gossip and discretion, flattery and faithful rebuke. Words build up or tear down a household and a city, and restraint in speech is repeatedly treated as a mark of wisdom.

themes.title: Work, wealth, and the poor
themes.body: Proverbs praises diligence and warns the sluggard, but it also warns against trusting riches, against dishonest gain, and against oppressing the poor. It says that the LORD defends the needy and that kindness to the poor is lending to God. Wealth is a real good in the book, but always a lesser one than wisdom, righteousness, and a good name.

keyChapters.why: The prologue states the book's purpose and its motto, the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge, and Wisdom first raises her voice in the streets.
The call to trust in the LORD with all your heart, and the teaching on the LORD's discipline that Hebrews 12 applies to Christian suffering.
Wisdom's great speech, including her presence with God before and during creation, a passage central to later Jewish and Christian reflection on the Word and on Christ.
The two banquets of Wisdom and Folly bring the opening section to its decisive choice.
The start of the Solomonic sayings shows the book's typical form: short, contrasting two-line proverbs.
Contains the much-quoted saying on training a child and the beginning of the words of the wise, with their links to Egyptian instruction.
Lemuel's mother's counsel on justice for the poor and the acrostic poem of the woman of noble character that closes the book.
